Day 73 of 100 · Kubernetes

Kubernetes ReplicaSets

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityKubernetesPublished artifact recovered

ReplicaSets continuously maintain a requested number of matching Pods and recreate missing replicas from a Pod template.

Architecture / mental model

ReplicaSet desired replicas + selector → matching Pods
2/3 matching → controller creates 1 new Pod

How it works

A ReplicaSet has one core responsibility: keep a specified number of Pods matching its selector running.

The selector and Pod-template labels connect the controller to the workload. If desired state is three and only two matching Pods exist, the controller creates another Pod from the template.

Deleting one managed Pod is a useful demonstration of reconciliation: the controller notices actual state no longer equals desired state and replaces the missing replica.

Hands-on reference

kubectl apply -f replicaset.yaml
kubectl get rs
kubectl get pods -l app=web
kubectl describe rs web
kubectl delete pod POD_NAME
kubectl get pods -l app=web -w

Verification

Apply a three-replica ReplicaSet, delete one managed Pod and watch the controller restore the count. Confirm the replacement is a new Pod rather than the deleted object returning from the dead, because Kubernetes has boundaries even if YAML occasionally looks supernatural.

Field note / gotcha

Selector and template labels must agree. A mismatch can make a controller fail validation or manage a different set of Pods than the operator intended.

Security considerations

Replica count is availability logic, not access control. Apply Pod security, service-account and network policies separately.

What I learned

Controllers are Kubernetes' core mental model: state is maintained by reconciliation, not by hoping individual processes remain alive forever.
